Hormuz: Iran says it has reached an understanding with Oman to manage the strait, which will “never” return to how it was before the war

In an interview with Al Jazeera published on November 11, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of the Iranian Parliament and chief negotiator, says he has reached an understanding with Oman on shipping routes through Hormuz. The same day, a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in the eastern part of the strait [1][2][5].

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Strait of Hormuz would “never” return to its status before the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran [1][4]. “There are no free waters,” he summed up [3].

He announced: “We have reached an understanding with Oman on the shipping corridor and the traffic separation scheme in the Strait of Hormuz” [2]. According to one account, this understanding is part of Iran’s seven-point peace proposal [3].

For Ghalibaf, the rules of the strait fall under the laws of the two coastal states, Iran and Oman, and the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea does not apply there: the strait would therefore not be international waters [3][4]. At this stage, this understanding is known only through his own account [1][2].

He restated Tehran’s preconditions: lifting of the US naval blockade and sanctions, release of frozen Iranian assets, an end to fighting on all fronts and an explicit announcement that the war is over [3]. According to him, these points stem from the Islamabad memorandum signed in June and must be implemented before any negotiation [3].

Iran says it has sent its response to Washington through Qatar, the mediator, and is awaiting an official reply; Ghalibaf believes that “the ball is in the American court” and blames the “lack of trust” in the United States for blocking a deal [4][9].

Early on Wednesday, November 11, according to the Iranian army, a tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine in a “dangerous and prohibited” area in the eastern part of the strait [5][6]. The Iranian navy warned shipowners that safe passage requires coordination with its armed forces [5].

The day before, the Revolutionary Guards had reported three tankers on fire, one of which had hit a mine [7]. Ships had already been hit by mines on November 7 and 8, according to Iranian media [5][7].
Key takeaway: Iran wants to turn its grip on Hormuz into a lasting rule, shared with Oman, rather than a mere wartime blockade [1][2][3].
It is a direct challenge to the principle of free passage: before the war, about 130 ships crossed the strait every day, and Tehran now wants every passage to take place on its terms [8][5].
Mines change the nature of the risk: even without a targeted attack, a ship that strays from the routes set by Iran can blow up, which weighs on insurers and shipowners [5][7].
On the diplomatic front, Tehran demands that its conditions be met first, while Donald Trump talks of “positive momentum” toward the end of the war [3][10].

For you in France, this means that the strait through which a large share of Gulf oil passes may remain under Iranian control even after a deal. Fuel prices could therefore stay sensitive to the slightest incident in the area for a long time.

Ukraine: Abu Dhabi ends with an exchange of more than 1,000 prisoners on each side, no ceasefire, and US envoys head off to see Putin

On Wednesday, November 11, after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, Russians and Ukrainians agreed “in principle” on a large prisoner exchange, more than 1,000 on each side. Nothing, however, on a ceasefire or territory. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are leaving to see Vladimir Putin in Moscow [1][3][5].

The talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States, held in the United Arab Emirates, ended on Wednesday, November 11 after two days of discussions [1][6]. They were the first negotiations between Russians and Ukrainians in nine months [1].

The only concrete result: an agreement in principle on a large-scale exchange of prisoners of war, covering more than 1,000 people on each side [5]. Jared Kushner, US envoy and Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said the exact number would be settled on Thursday, November 12 [3][4].

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, confirmed the agreement, specifying that it was “in principle” [3]. On the Russian side, General Alexander Zorin estimated, according to the TASS agency, that the exchange could take place within two to three weeks [1][3].
On substance, no breakthrough: no ceasefire and no compromise on territory, which remains the main sticking point [2][3]. Vladimir Medinsky warned that Russia would not give up its demands [1].
Ukraine is still awaiting Moscow’s response to its proposed truce for ships carrying grain in the Black Sea [1].

Next step: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s special envoy, are traveling to Moscow to meet Vladimir Putin in order to “try to make progress on some of the issues we discussed,” according to Kushner, then to Dublin to brief Volodymyr Zelensky [1][2]. The Ukrainian president arrived there on Thursday for the European Political Community summit [7].
Jared Kushner also said he wanted to broaden the format of the talks into a multilateral negotiation, including the European Union and NATO [2].

Key takeaway: the prisoner exchange is the first concrete gesture between Moscow and Kyiv after nine months of silence, but it settles nothing of substance, as the two sides remain far apart on territory and political conditions [1][3].

The Moscow-then-Dublin trip shows Washington’s role as intermediary: the US envoys will take the issues raised in Abu Dhabi to Vladimir Putin, then report back to Volodymyr Zelensky, just as nearly 50 European leaders gather in Ireland [1][7].
If it materializes, the idea of involving the European Union and NATO would bring Europeans to the table, whereas the Abu Dhabi talks were held between Americans, Russians and Ukrainians [1][2].
The Black Sea track has a direct economic stake: a truce for grain cargo ships would protect Ukraine’s agricultural exports without waiting for a comprehensive peace deal [1].

For you, nothing changes right away: a peace deal is not in sight. But the outcome of these talks weighs on what Europe, and therefore France, will still have to pay to support Ukraine, and on energy and grain prices if fighting in the Black Sea calms down.

Nearly 50 European leaders in Dublin with Zelensky, ahead of an EU summit on the €70 billion requested by Kyiv

On Thursday, November 12, Dublin hosts the 9th summit of the European Political Community: 48 heads of state and government invited, including Volodymyr Zelensky, to discuss security, energy and democracy. On Friday, EU leaders move on to Ukraine’s funding in 2027, which is stalled by the German ultimatum [1][5][8][9].

The 9th summit of the European Political Community (EPC), a forum bringing together EU countries and their neighbors on the continent, is being held on Thursday, November 12 at the Convention Centre Dublin [1][2]. The Council of the EU counts 48 heads of state and government invited; the Irish government speaks of more than 50 leaders [1][3].

It is co-chaired by António Costa, President of the European Council, and by Irish Prime Minister (Taoiseach) Micheál Martin, under the theme “Europe: strong, secure and connected” [1][2]. On the agenda: competitiveness (innovation, connections and energy) and the defense of democracy [1].

According to Agence Europe, the debates focus largely on the continent’s security challenges, particularly Ukraine [4]. The Irish police describe it as the largest gathering of heads of state and government ever held in the country [10].

Volodymyr Zelensky has arrived in Dublin, where he plans talks with around twenty leaders [5]. He is also awaiting a briefing from US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner after their visit to Moscow, which follows the end of the Abu Dhabi talks [5][6].

On Friday, November 13, an informal meeting of the 27 EU heads of state and government, with the presidents of the Commission and the European Council, will follow at the same venue, for a strategic discussion without any formal decision [7].

This session is to focus on Ukraine’s growing financial needs: Volodymyr Zelensky is asking for an additional €70 billion for 2027 [8]. Leaders are also due to discuss artificial intelligence and who will represent the EU in future peace negotiations with Russia and Ukraine [8].

The financial file has been stuck since German Chancellor Friedrich Merz threatened to reject the 2028-2034 EU budget if all member states do not commit to funding Ukraine over the long term [9]. He is targeting four reluctant countries: Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic [11].
Key takeaway: Dublin is the first major European meeting after the Abu Dhabi talks, and Europe is looking for its place there while US envoys shuttle between Moscow and Kyiv [5][6][8].

The question of who will speak on behalf of the EU in future peace negotiations is on Friday’s agenda: without a designated representative, the 27 have no single voice facing the Americans, Russians and Ukrainians [8].
Money is the summit’s other crux: the €70 billion requested by Kyiv for 2027 has to be found while Berlin now links the EU’s long-term budget to a commitment by all member states to Ukraine [8][9].

For you, these two days partly decide what France will pay for Ukraine through the EU budget, and Europe’s place in any eventual peace, which matters for the continent’s security and for energy prices.

After the heat waves, Lecornu unveils a €500 million to €700 million plan for agriculture, dependent on the budget vote

On Thursday, November 12, the government presents the recovery plan promised to farmers after a summer of record heat waves: €500 million to €700 million to adapt livestock farms to the heat, store water and fund “projects for the future.” But everything depends on the 2027 budget, rejected by MPs in early November [1][3][8].

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was due to detail its content on Thursday, November 12, at the close of the “food sovereignty conferences” [1][2]. These conferences had been launched a year earlier by Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard at the Rungis market, where she called for an “awakening” in the face of the “agricultural war” [2].

The package, worth €500 million to €700 million, had been announced on October 15 at Matignon and is to be included in the 2027 state budget [3][7]. It comes on top of the €1 billion emergency plan announced in early September [1].
The climate component funds insulation and ventilation of livestock buildings, as well as water storage with tanks, to avoid reliving the summer of 2026 [1].

The second component supports “projects for the future” to produce more in sectors deemed priorities: about 900 project proposals have already been identified according to AFP, 800 according to Pleinchamp [1][4]. Calls for applications are being launched in the regions, and projects will be selected by committees chaired by the prefect and the regional president [1].
The plan also includes a pact on farm succession, that is, the takeover of farms by new farmers [4].
On October 15, Sébastien Lecornu had warned that the deficit must not exceed 5% of GDP at year-end: if aid to farmers increases, savings will be made in other sectors [7].
Annie Genevard warns that implementation depends on the vote on the 2027 budget in the Senate: “Without a budget, we will put farmers in very serious difficulty” [1][5].
Key takeaway: this is the state’s main response to the agricultural crisis after the summer heat waves, but its money does not exist yet, since the 2027 budget has not been passed [1][5].

On November 4, the National Assembly rejected the revenue part of the budget by 458 votes to none, and the bill goes to the Senate in its original version [8]. On November 3, before senators, Annie Genevard acknowledged that the plan had not been finalized and was not included in the initial draft budget [6].
The number of projects that will come to fruition remains uncertain: the law’s impact assessment mentions a target of around fifty projects by 2027, far from the hundreds of proposals identified [1].
The plan targets both adaptation to global warming and “food sovereignty,” that is, the country’s ability to produce itself what it considers essential to feed itself [2].

For you, this plan can make a difference on store shelves: livestock and crops that better withstand scorching summers mean French products (meat, milk, fruit) less exposed to shortages and price spikes. But it remains dependent on the budget vote in the Senate.

China: Beijing vows to defend Cuba against US sanctions, but treads carefully with Washington ahead of the Shenzhen summit

On Wednesday, November 11, Wang Yi promised Cuba China’s “firm support” against sanctions, six days after Washington sanctioned two Chinese companies accused of equipping the Cuban military. The same day, he assured Marco Rubio that Beijing wanted to strengthen cooperation ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting on November 18 and 19 [1][3][5].

On November 5, the State Department sanctioned two Chinese companies, China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies, accused of supplying components and equipment to the Cuban armed forces via the Cuban buyer Sociedad Mercantil Duna [3][4]. CEIEC had already been under sanctions since November 2020 for its activities in Venezuela [4].

The package targets a total of eight entities and two individuals linked to Cuba’s financial, maritime and military procurement networks; five vessels from its oil network are also blocked [3][8]. The US Treasury has also given itself the right to sanction any foreign company active in electronics, industry, shipping or technology in Cuba, under Executive Order 14404 [4].
Beijing condemned these sanctions and promised to take “all necessary measures” to protect its companies [7][8].

On Wednesday in Beijing, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi received his Cuban counterpart Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, in China from November 10 to 13 as a special envoy: “China will firmly support Cuba in defending its national sovereignty […] and in its opposition to sanctions, blockades and external interference” [1][2][7]. The Chinese readout does not name the United States [2].

Bruno Rodríguez called the US measures an “oil blockade,” thanked China for its energy assistance and reaffirmed the one-China principle [2]. He also met Wang Huning, one of the Communist Party’s top leaders [2].

The same day, on the phone with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Wang Yi said he was ready to “properly manage differences and sensitive issues” and described the stability of relations as “hard-won”; Beijing called the exchange “constructive” [5][6][9].

This call prepares the expected meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit, on November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, where a three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin is also under discussion [5][10].
Key takeaway: China is playing both sides, with open support for Cuba on one hand and a conciliatory tone with Washington on the other, one week before a summit it is hosting [1][5].
For the first time, Chinese companies are targeted by US sanctions against Cuba, making the island a new point of friction between the two powers [7][4].

The trade truce remains fragile: Beijing has just extended by two months its pause on certain critical mineral controls, but Washington is demanding that it honor its commitments on rare earths, which some companies say they are short of [11][12].

For you, this double game matters because a successful Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen could extend the trade truce and secure rare earths, used in the electric cars, wind turbines and electronics you buy. A flare-up over Cuba would complicate this rapprochement.

War with Iran: J.D. Vance considers a face-to-face meeting with a regime hard-liner, but Tehran denies any negotiation

According to the Wall Street Journal, as reported on Wednesday, November 11, US Vice President J.D. Vance, tasked by Donald Trump with negotiating with Iran, is considering a direct meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s security chief. One possible trade-off is circulating: less US military pressure in exchange for letting 25 tankers through Hormuz. Iran denies it [1][2][3].

According to the Wall Street Journal, Donald Trump authorized J.D. Vance to lead negotiations with Iran, and the vice president wrote to Mohsen Rezaei in October to request a meeting [1][3]. No date has been set and discussions about this face-to-face meeting remain “preliminary” [1][3].
Doha, the capital of Qatar, has been mentioned as a possible venue; in the meantime, the two sides continue to talk through intermediaries, Qatar and Pakistan [1][2].

According to the newspaper, the mediators are proposing a trade-off: the United States would move its aircraft carriers away and ease the blockade of Iranian ports, and Iran would let 25 tankers through the Strait of Hormuz [1][5]. Neither side has confirmed this proposal [3].

In Tehran, Mohsen Rezaei called reports of a meeting “completely false” and spoke of “imaginary negotiations”; he insists that no talks are under way with Washington [2][4]. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied any plan for a meeting [2].

Iran says it is awaiting the US response to its seven conditions for negotiating, including the lifting of sanctions and the naval blockade and an end to fighting on all fronts; as long as they are not met, the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed, according to Mohsen Rezaei [2].

In Washington, the administration is divided: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff, want to keep up the pressure on Iran until it makes concessions [1][3].
After hosting the Prime Minister of Qatar, Donald Trump said a resumption of full-scale war soon was unlikely, but still rejects the Iranian truce plan [2].

Key takeaway: Washington is looking for a way out of the war with Iran by handing the file to the vice president, but Tehran refuses to admit it is negotiating. The concrete stake is the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran ties to its seven conditions [1][2].

The choice of Mohsen Rezaei is no accident: he is a hard-line interlocutor, and he is already warning that Iran will not give up its enriched uranium [3][5]. A direct meeting with an official at this level would be a break after months of indirect contacts [1].

The 25-tanker proposal shows the logic of a possible deal: oil flowing out of the Gulf in exchange for a US military pullback [1][5]. But in the White House, the advocates of pressure, Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller, carry a lot of weight, and nothing is settled [1][3].

For you, every signal of opening or deadlock around Hormuz quickly shows up at the pump: part of the world’s oil passes through this strait, and its closure pushes up the price of a barrel, and therefore of gasoline and heating in France.

Germany: Merz’s coalition postpones the soda tax, scraps the plastic tax and stalls on cutting the electricity tax

On Wednesday, November 11, the conservatives and Social Democrats governing in Berlin reached compromises on the 2027 budget: the tax on sugary drinks slips to early 2028, and the one on plastic packaging is dropped for 2027. But the general cut in the electricity tax, estimated at €5.4 billion, remains unfunded [1][2][3].

Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition, which brings together the Union (CDU-CSU) and the SPD, agreed on several points of the 2027 federal budget, according to coalition sources quoted by the German press [1][3][4].
The tax on very sugary drinks will come into force in early 2028, rather than in July 2027 as planned in the initial draft, i.e., a few months later [1][2].
The new tax on plastic packaging will not be levied in 2027 [1][3]. Euronews sees it as a setback for Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil [1].

The coalition failed to agree on a general cut in the electricity tax (Stromsteuer) for households and businesses [2][3]. Bringing it down to the minimum allowed by the EU would cost about €5.4 billion, and no funding has been found [3].
Opinions differ on what comes next: for t-online, a general cut is becoming increasingly unlikely; according to ZDF, negotiations on this point are continuing [2][3].
Some planned social savings are being abandoned, including the cut to the immediate supplement for children from low-income households (Kindersofortzuschlag) [3][4].
The final changes will be decided at the budget committee session, ahead of a vote in the Bundestag at the end of November [2][3].

Key takeaway: the EU’s largest economy is struggling to finalize its 2027 budget, and it is the electricity tax cut for everyone, households and businesses alike, that pays the price for lack of €5.4 billion [2][3].

The tax postponements show the coalition’s delicate balance: dropping the plastic tax and postponing the soda tax deprive the state of revenue, while withdrawing some social cuts adds spending [1][3].

This German budget is being debated while Friedrich Merz threatens to block the 2028-2034 EU budget if all member states do not commit to funding Ukraine, targeting Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic [5][6].
For low-income households, dropping the cut to the Kindersofortzuschlag avoids a loss of support; for beverage and packaging manufacturers, the new taxes are postponed [1][3].

For you, Germany is a major trading partner of France: if its companies do not see electricity prices fall, their business, and therefore their purchases of French products, could suffer. And the French debate on taxes in the 2027 budget has its counterpart on the other side of the Rhine.

Rail: the state signs a €4.5 billion-a-year contract with SNCF Réseau to renovate the tracks, but the funding has yet to be found

On Thursday, November 12 in Trappes (Yvelines), Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot signs with SNCF Réseau the contract governing the maintenance of the rail network until 2033. It provides €4.5 billion a year to renovate and modernize the tracks from 2028, about €1.5 billion more, but the regulator is concerned about the funding [1][2][3].
Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot signs the performance contract with SNCF Réseau CEO Matthieu Chabanel, in the presence of Jean Castex, CEO of the SNCF group, according to the ministry [1][2].
The signing, in Trappes, is followed by a visit to a worksite renewing 13 km of rails between Clamart and Trappes [1][2].
This contract covers the 2024-2033 period and sets out the commitments of the state and SNCF Réseau, the company that manages the tracks, for the maintenance and modernization of the network [3].

It provides for €4.5 billion of investment a year from 2028 in regeneration, that is, replacing worn tracks and overhead lines, and in modernizing the network [2][6]. The Transport Regulatory Authority (ART) sees it as an additional effort of about €1.5 billion a year [3].
The government presents it as “a historic commitment” and “unprecedented,” in response to “the French people’s appetite for trains” [1][4].

SNCF Réseau must itself contribute €500 million a year, and a large share of the funding is deferred to later decisions [5]. According to Politique Matin, the €4.5 billion remains “subject to the financial trajectory” [2].
The ART welcomes the investment effort but calls for its funding to be secured; it considers the contract insufficiently incentivizing on performance and questions some financial assumptions [3].
Key takeaway: this contract commits the state to upgrading the rail network for a decade, but a good part of the money depends on budget choices that have not yet been made [3][5].

The worksite visited on Thursday illustrates the concrete stake: 13 km of rails renewed on a Paris suburban line, between Clamart and Trappes, the kind of work the contract is meant to multiply [1][2].

The budget context makes the promise fragile: on November 4, the National Assembly rejected the revenue part of the 2027 budget by 458 votes to none, and the ART is precisely calling for the funding to be secured [3][7].
The text had first been put out for consultation; the government had then announced the approach without specifying the funding, according to Ville, Rail & Transports [5].

For you, if you take the train, the TER or the RER, this contract partly decides the condition of the tracks in the coming years, and therefore delays, slowdowns and works. If it is really funded, renovation works will multiply from 2028.

Morocco: Jean-Noël Barrot in Rabat to prepare an unprecedented treaty, two weeks after the end of the UN mission in Western Sahara

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot is expected in Morocco this Thursday, November 12 to meet Nasser Bourita and take part in the Global Women’s Forum for Peace in Essaouira. His visit comes just after the expiry of the mandate of MINURSO, the UN mission in Western Sahara [1][2][5].
The Quai d’Orsay announced this trip at its press briefing on November 5; according to North Africa Post, Jean-Noël Barrot was due to arrive on Thursday, November 12 [1][6].

The minister is to hold talks with his Moroccan counterpart Nasser Bourita on French-Moroccan cooperation and major international issues; the exact agenda of the talks in Rabat has not been made public [2][3][7].
He will also take part in the Global Women’s Forum for Peace, held in Essaouira from November 12 to 14 [1][2].
This trip follows the meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris on November 9 and 10, and the Paris Peace Forum on November 11 [8][4].

During his previous visit, on May 20, Jean-Noël Barrot had already met Nasser Bourita in Rabat to prepare an unprecedented bilateral treaty [3][4]. This text is to cover the economy and industry, security and defense, culture and the French-speaking world, as well as political geostrategy [4][8].

On October 30, the UN Security Council adopted neither of the two texts on Western Sahara, and MINURSO’s mandate expired, a first since 1991 [9][10]. Its liquidation was made official on November 1 [10].
According to La Relève, Jean-Noël Barrot’s visit comes precisely after this expiry of the mandate [5].
Key takeaway: Paris wants to turn its rapprochement with Rabat into a treaty, a rare framework that would bind the two countries on the economy as well as on defense [3][4].
The timing is sensitive: the end of MINURSO, a first since 1991 after a Russian veto, opens a period of uncertainty in Western Sahara [9][10][5].
By coming to Rabat just after the UN mandate expired, Paris is sending a strong political signal on an issue where every visit is closely interpreted [5][4].
For Morocco, this visit confirms an “exceptional partnership” with France, as Rabat and Paris hold meeting after meeting to finalize the treaty [4][3].
For you, this future treaty could weigh on everyday issues: trade, French companies setting up in Morocco, cooperation on security and migration, and ties with Moroccans living in France.
